claim: The defined diet led to lifespan extension in Drosophila males.
source: The defined diet, which was prepared from chemical components and mimicked dietary restriction conditions (Bass et al., 2007), led to lifespan extension (Figure 1A), similar to the well-characterized effect of dietary restriction (Mair et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A showing lifespan curves, citations to previous work on dietary restriction effects, and experimental data from the study.

claim: Mean lifespan of flies on standard diet was 50.8 days.
source: Mean lifespan of flies on standard and defined diets was 50.8 and 64.4 days, respectively (log-rank test [p<0.001]).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by experimental measurements reported in the text with statistical significance.

claim: Mean lifespan of flies on defined diet was 64.4 days.
source: Mean lifespan of flies on standard and defined diets was 50.8 and 64.4 days, respectively (log-rank test [p<0.001]).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by experimental measurements reported in the text with statistical significance.

claim: The number of detected nontargeted metabolites increases with age in Drosophila.
source: We found that the number of detected metabolites was lowest in the young flies in each dietary group and increased as a function of age (repeated measures ANOVA, p<6 × 10−6 for each diet).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (repeated measures ANOVA) of experimental data across age groups.

claim: The overall metabolite signal slightly decreased throughout lifespan.
source: On the other hand, the overall signal (the sum of signals for all molecular species detected) slightly decreased throughout lifespan (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: The rise in the number of detected metabolites leveled off at the most advanced ages.
source: Interestingly, the rise in the number of detected metabolites was steady during adulthood, yet leveled off (and even slightly decreased) at the most advanced ages (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data visualization in Figure 1A and textual description of the pattern.

claim: The transition in metabolite diversity corresponded to the late-life transition in the lifespan curves and mortality.
source: This transition in the metabolite diversity corresponded to the late-life transition in the lifespan curves and mortality (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting relationship between metabolite diversity and the aging process.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of metabolite diversity patterns with mortality data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Analysis of metabolite diversity using a panel of 205 known metabolites did not show significant age-associated trends.
source: In contrast, analysis of metabolite diversity using a panel of 205 known metabolites did not show significant age-associated trends (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by targeted metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The distribution of signal intensities between targeted metabolites and metabolites showing diversity fluctuations differed by few orders of magnitude.
source: Furthermore, the distribution of signal intensities between targeted metabolites and metabolites, which show diversity fluctuations throughout lifespan were different by few orders of magnitude (Figure 1B,C), suggesting that the latter generally corresponded to molecules of low abundance and were not due to errors of detection.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of signal intensity distributions shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Metabolites showing diversity fluctuations generally corresponded to molecules of low abundance.
source: Furthermore, the distribution of signal intensities between targeted metabolites and metabolites, which show diversity fluctuations throughout lifespan were different by few orders of magnitude (Figure 1B,C), suggesting that the latter generally corresponded to molecules of low abundance and were not due to errors of detection.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the difference in signal intensity distributions shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Changes in metabolite diversity could not be attributable to the presence of yeast-derived metabolites in the diet.
source: Also, changes in metabolite diversity could not be attributable to the presence of yeast-derived metabolites in our diet, since the chemically defined diet contained no cellular products.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental design using a chemically defined diet without cellular products.

claim: The metabolite profiling platform detected >15,000 unique analytes.
source: Our metabolite profiling platform detected >15,000 unique analytes (nontargeted, non-redundant, de-isotoped LC-MS peaks), whose relative abundance was followed as a function of age.
evidence: The claim is directly stated based on the LC-MS profiling methodology used in the study.

claim: 2234 metabolites were identified as age-associated in the standard diet.
source: Using repeated measures ANOVA and stringent statistical cut-off that estimated <0.2% of false positives ('Materials and methods'), we identified 2234 and 2216 metabolites (∼14% of all detected metabolites) that qualified as age-associated in the standard and defined diets, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (repeated measures ANOVA) of the metabolite profiling data.

claim: 2216 metabolites were identified as age-associated in the defined diet.
source: Using repeated measures ANOVA and stringent statistical cut-off that estimated <0.2% of false positives ('Materials and methods'), we identified 2234 and 2216 metabolites (∼14% of all detected metabolites) that qualified as age-associated in the standard and defined diets, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (repeated measures ANOVA) of the metabolite profiling data.

claim: Approximately 14% of all detected metabolites qualified as age-associated.
source: Using repeated measures ANOVA and stringent statistical cut-off that estimated <0.2% of false positives ('Materials and methods'), we identified 2234 and 2216 metabolites (∼14% of all detected metabolites) that qualified as age-associated in the standard and defined diets, respectively.
evidence: The claim is directly stated based on statistical analysis of the metabolite data.

claim: 1,066 age-associated metabolites were common to both dietary regimens.
source: Of the detected age-associated features, 1,066 were common to both dietary regimens (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Common age-associated metabolites exhibited very similar trajectories of change between the two diets with median Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.76.
source: These molecules exhibited very similar trajectories of change between the two diets (median Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.76), in contrast to the lack of such correlation when using all metabolite pairs between the diets (permutation test p<0.001) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PCA of between-group scaled values segregated samples first by diet and then by age.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the between-group scaled values segregated samples first by diet and then by age (Figure 2C), suggesting that the magnitudes of these metabolites were affected by dietary conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: PCA of within-group scaled data revealed an age-dependent, but diet-independent segregation.
source: On the other hand, PCA of the within-group scaled data revealed an age-dependent, but diet-independent segregation, with the replicate samples of both diets grouping closely together (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Most age-related changes in metabolite levels within individual diets did not exceed 4–8-fold across lifespan.
source: Furthermore, most age-related changes in metabolite intensity (levels hereafter for simplicity) within individual diets did not exceed 4–8-fold across lifespan (Figure 3A,B), which was consistent with the differences in gene expression between Drosophila subjected to dietary restriction or stress (Zou et al., 2000; Pletcher et al., 2002; Girardot et al., 2004; Landis et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by fold-change analysis shown in Figure 3A,B and comparison with previous gene expression studies.

claim: 76% of age-related metabolites common to both diets showed less than twofold changes between the two diets.
source: Specifically, among the 1,542 age-related metabolites common to both diets, 76% showed less than twofold changes between the two diets (Figure 4A), indicating that the influence of diet was noticeable, but mostly small in magnitude.
evidence: The claim is supported by inter-dietary fold-change analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was high prevalence of strong correlations (both positive and negative) between individual metabolite levels across lifespan and lifespan curves.
source: These age-related changes may be linked to longevity as there was high prevalence of strong correlations (both positive and negative) between individual metabolite levels across lifespan and lifespan curves (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A very large fraction of metabolites that decreased with age was derived from the lipid fraction in both diets.
source: Interestingly, a very large fraction of metabolites that decreased with age was derived from the lipid fraction, and this observation applied to both diets (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Lipid profiles declined with age in other animals.
source: Lipid profiles also declined with age in other animals (Houtkooper et al., 2011; Lapierre et al., 2011; Singh and Cuervo, 2012), suggesting that our analysis captures a general scheme of age-related changes in lipid metabolism.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in other animal models.

claim: Most polar metabolites increased with age and their rates of change between the diets were more dynamic.
source: In contrast, most polar metabolites increased with age and their rates of change between the diets were more dynamic (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 1172 age-associated genes (ca. 8% of total) were common to both diets in the gene expression analysis.
source: By applying similar statistical methods as those used for identifying the age-associated metabolites, we identified 1172 age-associated genes (ca. 8% of total) common to both diets (repeated measures ANOVA, p<0.0013).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of gene expression data.

claim: About 70% of age-related genes featured gradual transitions throughout lifespan, both increasing and decreasing with age.
source: Clustering analysis revealed that about 70% of age-related genes also featured gradual transitions throughout lifespan, both increasing (clusters 2 through 5) and decreasing (clusters 6 through 8) with age (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis of gene expression data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Longevity in dietary restricted flies was associated with reduced metabolism.
source: We used Gene ontology (GO) (Ashburner et al., 2000) to test for enrichment of biological processes within each cluster and found that longevity in dietary restricted (DR) flies was associated with reduced metabolism (cluster 2), increased transport (cluster 11) and altered response to pathogens, albeit early in life (cluster 4) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Longevity in dietary restricted flies was associated with increased transport.
source: We used Gene ontology (GO) (Ashburner et al., 2000) to test for enrichment of biological processes within each cluster and found that longevity in dietary restricted (DR) flies was associated with reduced metabolism (cluster 2), increased transport (cluster 11) and altered response to pathogens, albeit early in life (cluster 4) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Longevity in dietary restricted flies was associated with altered response to pathogens early in life.
source: We used Gene ontology (GO) (Ashburner et al., 2000) to test for enrichment of biological processes within each cluster and found that longevity in dietary restricted (DR) flies was associated with reduced metabolism (cluster 2), increased transport (cluster 11) and altered response to pathogens, albeit early in life (cluster 4) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Genes with increased levels in cluster 1 were enriched for stress response genes.
source: Similarly to previous studies in mammals and other species, genes with increased levels in cluster 1 were enriched for stress response genes, whose expression rose at slower rate in DR flies, suggesting that improved homeostasis in these individuals may reduce the need for certain stress protection (Lee et al., 1999; de Magalhaes et al., 2009; Plank et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis and comparison with previous studies.

claim: Stress response gene expression rose at slower rate in DR flies.
source: Similarly to previous studies in mammals and other species, genes with increased levels in cluster 1 were enriched for stress response genes, whose expression rose at slower rate in DR flies, suggesting that improved homeostasis in these individuals may reduce the need for certain stress protection (Lee et al., 1999; de Magalhaes et al., 2009; Plank et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of gene expression trajectories and comparison with previous studies.

claim: Diet-independent effects predominated in transcript changes, making up 68% of age-related genes.
source: The diet-independent effects, however, predominated (68%) and fell into clusters 4, 5 and 7.
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis of gene expression data.

claim: Diet-independent metabolite changes made up 62% of total age-related signals common to both diets.
source: Strikingly, we observed similar frequencies for age-related metabolites whereby clusters 2, 3, 6 and 10 can be categorized as diet-independent making up to 62% of total age-related signals common to both diets.
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis of metabolite data.

claim: Age-related changes in either gene expression or metabolite levels were delayed in long-living flies.
source: Interestingly, these age-related changes (both increases and decreases common to both diets) in either gene expression or metabolite levels were delayed in long-living flies (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Metabolome remodeling was decelerated with age within each dietary group.
source: Moreover, metabolome remodeling represented by these signals was decelerated with age within each dietary group (i.e., the signals initially showed robust changes, but then almost leveled off).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of metabolite trajectory patterns across age.

claim: 81 metabolites displayed age-associated trends under both dietary regimens among 205 annotated metabolites.
source: Among these, 81 metabolites displayed age-associated trends under both dietary regimens (repeated one-way ANOVA, p<0.05) and were associated with biosynthesis of amino acids, lipids, energy homeostasis, and damage production (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of targeted metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Eighty percent of metabolites in cluster 1 were triglycerides (TAGs) and diacylglycerols (DAGs).
source: Eighty percent of metabolites in this cluster were triglycerides (TAGs) and diacylglycerols (DAGs), all of which normally rise highly during larval growth but decline thereafter (Carvalho et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolite identification and comparison with previous developmental studies.

claim: TAGs and DAGs normally rise highly during larval growth but decline thereafter.
source: Eighty percent of metabolites in this cluster were triglycerides (TAGs) and diacylglycerols (DAGs), all of which normally rise highly during larval growth but decline thereafter (Carvalho et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous developmental studies.

claim: Age-associated tendencies suggest increased synthesis (or reduced utilization) of lipids in long-living flies.
source: Also, the age-associated tendencies between our standard and DR-like regimens suggest increased synthesis (or reduced utilization) of lipids in long-living flies and agree with higher lipid stores and starvation resistance of DR flies in previous studies (Burger et al., 2007; Katewa et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is inferred from metabolite trajectory analysis and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A progressive age-associated increase in cholesteryl esters was observed in long-living flies compared to controls.
source: In contrast, we observed a progressive age-associated increase in the cholesteryl esters in our long-living flies compared to controls (cluster 11).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolite profiling data showing cluster 11 patterns.

claim: Accumulation of cholesteryl esters may extend Drosophila lifespan via increased pathogen protection.
source: While accumulation of this lipid class has been inferred to negatively affect mammalian fitness (Lawton et al., 2008), it may extend Drosophila lifespan via increased pathogen protection (Caragata et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on cholesteryl esters in different organisms.

claim: Downregulated metabolites in long-lived flies (clusters 5–8, n = 39) were associated with insulin signaling, energy homeostasis, and amino acid metabolism.
source: Second, consistent with the effects of dietary restriction, we find that downregulated metabolites in long-lived flies (clusters 5–8, n = 39) were associated with insulin signaling, energy homeostasis, and amino acid metabolism (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolite set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Methionine sulfoxide was elevated in long-lived but not in control flies.
source: Third, a striking observation was the elevation of methionine sulfoxide, which represents damage (Orentreich et al., 1993; Ruan et al., 2002; Koc et al., 2004), and taurine, a product of cysteine degradation and a component of bile acids (Massie et al., 1989; Brosnan and Brosnan, 2006), in long-lived but not in control flies (cluster 9, Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by targeted metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 7D and citations to previous studies.

claim: Taurine was elevated in long-lived but not in control flies.
source: Third, a striking observation was the elevation of methionine sulfoxide, which represents damage (Orentreich et al., 1993; Ruan et al., 2002; Koc et al., 2004), and taurine, a product of cysteine degradation and a component of bile acids (Massie et al., 1989; Brosnan and Brosnan, 2006), in long-lived but not in control flies (cluster 9, Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by targeted metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 7D and citations to previous studies.

claim: Methionine sulfoxide represents damage.
source: Third, a striking observation was the elevation of methionine sulfoxide, which represents damage (Orentreich et al., 1993; Ruan et al., 2002; Koc et al., 2004), and taurine, a product of cysteine degradation and a component of bile acids (Massie et al., 1989; Brosnan and Brosnan, 2006), in long-lived but not in control flies (cluster 9, Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on methionine sulfoxide.

claim: Taurine is a product of cysteine degradation and a component of bile acids.
source: Third, a striking observation was the elevation of methionine sulfoxide, which represents damage (Orentreich et al., 1993; Ruan et al., 2002; Koc et al., 2004), and taurine, a product of cysteine degradation and a component of bile acids (Massie et al., 1989; Brosnan and Brosnan, 2006), in long-lived but not in control flies (cluster 9, Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on taurine biochemistry.

claim: The levels of methionine sulfoxide and taurine started to decline at the point corresponding to high mortality in both groups.
source: The levels of these molecules started to decline at the point corresponding to high mortality in both groups (at 40 and 50 days, respectively), which may be due to the low levels of these metabolites in cohorts surviving to old age (Curtsinger et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolite trajectory data and citation to previous work on late-life mortality patterns.

claim: Tryptophan is a lifespan limiting amino acid.
source: Tryptophan is also a lifespan limiting amino acid (De Marte and Enesco, 1986) and a member of that cluster showing a similar pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study on tryptophan and lifespan.

claim: Degradation of tryptophan and rise of the downstream metabolite kynurenine were reported in older individuals.
source: Such bell-shaped lifespan-associated curves are not surprising as degradation of tryptophan and rise of the downstream metabolite kynurenine (also lifespan limiting metabolite [Oxenkrug et al., 2011] expressed higher on the defined diet) were reported in older individuals (Moroni et al., 1988; Frick et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on tryptophan metabolism in aging.

claim: Kynurenine is a lifespan limiting metabolite.
source: Such bell-shaped lifespan-associated curves are not surprising as degradation of tryptophan and rise of the downstream metabolite kynurenine (also lifespan limiting metabolite [Oxenkrug et al., 2011] expressed higher on the defined diet) were reported in older individuals (Moroni et al., 1988; Frick et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous study on kynurenine and lifespan.

claim: The higher levels of methionine sulfoxide, tryptophan, and kynurenine in long-living flies are consistent with the notion that lifespan extension by dietary restricted regimen may increase damage tolerance.
source: In sum, the higher levels of methionine sulfoxide, tryptophan, and kynurenine in our long-living flies are consistent with the notion that lifespan extension by dietary restricted regimen may increase damage tolerance.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the metabolite profiling data and represents an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Aging is thought to be associated with increased molecular damage.
source: Aging is thought to be associated with increased molecular damage, but representative markers vary across conditions and organisms, making it difficult to assess properties of cumulative damage throughout lifespan.
evidence: The claim represents established scientific consensus on aging theories.

claim: Representative markers of molecular damage vary across conditions and organisms.
source: Aging is thought to be associated with increased molecular damage, but representative markers vary across conditions and organisms, making it difficult to assess properties of cumulative damage throughout lifespan.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about variability in damage markers.

claim: Lifespan of various model organisms can be extended genetically via perturbation of nutrient sensing.
source: For example, lifespan of various model organisms can be extended genetically via perturbation of nutrient sensing, pharmacologically by rapamycin treatment, or nutritionally by dietary restriction (Bishop and Guarente, 2007; Fontana et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on lifespan extension methods.

claim: Lifespan of various model organisms can be extended pharmacologically by rapamycin treatment.
source: For example, lifespan of various model organisms can be extended genetically via perturbation of nutrient sensing, pharmacologically by rapamycin treatment, or nutritionally by dietary restriction (Bishop and Guarente, 2007; Fontana et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on lifespan extension methods.

claim: Lifespan of various model organisms can be extended nutritionally by dietary restriction.
source: For example, lifespan of various model organisms can be extended genetically via perturbation of nutrient sensing, pharmacologically by rapamycin treatment, or nutritionally by dietary restriction (Bishop and Guarente, 2007; Fontana et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on lifespan extension methods.

claim: Up-regulation of stress response and repair pathways may promote longevity.
source: Up-regulation of stress response and repair pathways, often linked to conditions of mild stress or hormesis (Rattan, 2010), may also promote longevity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on hormesis and longevity.

claim: Aging involves damage accumulation including DNA mutations, errors in protein synthesis, unwanted posttranslational modifications, and metabolite by-products.
source: It is often discussed that aging involves damage accumulation, therein an increase in DNA mutations, errors in protein synthesis, unwanted posttranslational modifications, metabolite by-products and many other damage forms contribute to the aging process (Rattan, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on damage accumulation theories of aging.

claim: The source of damage is frequently linked to metabolic activities, such as those that produce reactive oxygen species.
source: The source of damage is frequently linked to metabolic activities, such as those that produce reactive oxygen species and increase oxidative modifications (Kirkwood and Austad, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on metabolic sources of damage.

claim: Studies identified robust transcriptional remodeling that accompanies the aging process.
source: The exact mechanisms responsible for tolerance against molecular damage are not fully understood, but studies identified robust transcriptional remodeling that accompanies the aging process (Lee et al., 1999; Zou et al., 2000; Pletcher et al., 2002; McCarroll et al., 2004; de Magalhaes et al., 2009; Somel et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous transcriptome studies on aging.

claim: Individual damage types vary across conditions and among species.
source: Another complication in such analyses is that individual damage types (e.g., mutations, lipofuscin accumulation, oxidative modifications) vary across conditions and among species (Rattan, 2008; Edman et al., 2009; de Magalhaes, 2012; Jonker et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on damage variability.

claim: Metabolite profiling was used to explore metabolic signatures of aging in young vs old mice using a set of markers.
source: Recently, metabolite profiling was used to explore metabolic signatures of aging in young vs old mice (Houtkooper et al., 2011; Tomas-Loba et al., 2013) using a set of markers, thereby confirming that aging is associated with alterations in nutrient sensing, lipid and amino acid metabolism, and redox homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous metabolomics studies in mice.

claim: Aging is associated with alterations in nutrient sensing, lipid and amino acid metabolism, and redox homeostasis.
source: Recently, metabolite profiling was used to explore metabolic signatures of aging in young vs old mice (Houtkooper et al., 2011; Tomas-Loba et al., 2013) using a set of markers, thereby confirming that aging is associated with alterations in nutrient sensing, lipid and amino acid metabolism, and redox homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous metabolomics studies.

claim: Damaged molecular species are expected to exhibit age-associated mass shifts.
source: For example, damaged molecular species are expected to exhibit age-associated mass shifts, which may be represented by an increase in metabolite diversity, potentially offering a larger repertoire of damage forms than analyzed previously.
evidence: The claim represents a logical inference about how damage would manifest in mass spectrometry data.

claim: Aging is characterized by gradual metabolome remodeling.
source: Thus, aging is characterized by gradual metabolome remodeling, and condition- and advanced age-associated deceleration of this remodeling is linked to mortality and molecular damage.
evidence: The claim represents a major conclusion from the study based on the metabolite profiling data.

claim: Condition- and advanced age-associated deceleration of metabolome remodeling is linked to mortality and molecular damage.
source: Thus, aging is characterized by gradual metabolome remodeling, and condition- and advanced age-associated deceleration of this remodeling is linked to mortality and molecular damage.
evidence: The claim represents a major conclusion from the study based on the metabolite profiling data and mortality patterns.

claim: Aging is associated with increased metabolite diversity.
source: We find that aging is associated with increased metabolite diversity and low-abundance molecules, suggesting they include cumulative damage.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by the nontargeted metabolite profiling data showing increasing numbers of detected metabolites with age.

claim: Low-abundance molecules that increase with age include cumulative damage.
source: We find that aging is associated with increased metabolite diversity and low-abundance molecules, suggesting they include cumulative damage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pattern of low-abundance metabolite accumulation with age.

claim: The number of detected compounds leveled-off in late-life.
source: Remarkably, the number of detected compounds leveled-off in late-life, and this pattern associated with survivorship.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by the metabolite diversity data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The leveling-off of detected compounds in late-life associated with survivorship.
source: Remarkably, the number of detected compounds leveled-off in late-life, and this pattern associated with survivorship.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of metabolite diversity patterns with lifespan curves.

claim: Fourteen percent of metabolites showed age-associated changes.
source: Fourteen percent of metabolites showed age-associated changes, which decelerated in late-life and long-lived flies.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by statistical analysis of the metabolite profiling data.

claim: Age-associated metabolite changes decelerated in late-life and long-lived flies.
source: Fourteen percent of metabolites showed age-associated changes, which decelerated in late-life and long-lived flies.
evidence: The claim is supported by trajectory analysis of age-associated metabolites.

claim: Known metabolites changed in abundance similarly to nontargeted metabolites and transcripts.
source: In contrast, known metabolites changed in abundance similarly to nontargeted metabolites and transcripts, but did not increase in diversity.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of targeted and nontargeted metabolite profiling data with transcriptome data.

claim: Known metabolites did not increase in diversity with age.
source: In contrast, known metabolites changed in abundance similarly to nontargeted metabolites and transcripts, but did not increase in diversity.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by the targeted metabolite profiling data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Targeted profiling revealed slower metabolism in long-lived flies.
source: Targeted profiling also revealed slower metabolism and accumulation of lifespan-limiting molecules.
evidence: The claim is supported by targeted metabolite profiling data and metabolite set enrichment analysis.

claim: Targeted profiling revealed accumulation of lifespan-limiting molecules in long-lived flies.
source: Targeted profiling also revealed slower metabolism and accumulation of lifespan-limiting molecules.
evidence: The claim is supported by targeted metabolite profiling data showing elevated levels of methionine sulfoxide, tryptophan, and kynurenine.

claim: Long-living species may feature higher levels of lifespan-limiting molecules.
source: We suggest that long-living species may also feature higher levels of lifespan-limiting molecules and that metabolome remodeling upon dietary interventions activates compensatory mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is a speculative extrapolation from the findings in Drosophila to other species.

claim: Metabolome remodeling upon dietary interventions activates compensatory mechanisms.
source: We suggest that long-living species may also feature higher levels of lifespan-limiting molecules and that metabolome remodeling upon dietary interventions activates compensatory mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of elevated damage markers in long-lived flies.

claim: A change in lifespan involves both a delay in age-related metabolome and gene expression remodeling and a change in the set of expressed metabolites and genes at any point throughout lifespan.
source: Together with the analyses that revealed the diet-associated changes in the metabolome composition, these findings suggested that a change in lifespan involves both a delay in age-related metabolome and gene expression remodeling and a change in the set of expressed metabolites and genes at any point throughout lifespan.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of metabolite and gene expression trajectories between control and long-lived flies.

claim: Lifespan extension by dietary restricted regimen may increase damage tolerance.
source: In sum, the higher levels of methionine sulfoxide, tryptophan, and kynurenine in our long-living flies are consistent with the notion that lifespan extension by dietary restricted regimen may increase damage tolerance.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of elevated damage markers in long-lived flies.

claim: Aging may be associated with cumulative damage, whereby mild effects of myriad damage forms may exhibit additive effects on organism's fitness.
source: However, aging may be associated with cumulative damage, whereby mild effects of the myriad damage forms may exhibit additive effects on organism's fitness.
evidence: The claim represents a theoretical framework for understanding aging and damage accumulation.

claim: In interventions that extend lifespan, reduction of some damage forms may be compensated by accumulation of other forms of damage.
source: For example, in interventions that extend lifespan (e.g., dietary restriction) reduction of some damage forms may be compensated by accumulation of other forms of damage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of elevated damage markers in long-lived flies despite lifespan extension.

claim: The extended metabolome composition may include by-products that affect viability and damage forms that reach detection thresholds during organism's aging.
source: The extended metabolome composition may include by-products that affect viability and damage forms that reach and pass the detection thresholds during organism's aging (Phoenix and de Grey, 2007), but they likely represent only the tip of the iceberg of cumulative damage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pattern of increasing metabolite diversity with age and supported by citation.

claim: Detected damage forms likely represent only the tip of the iceberg of cumulative damage.
source: The extended metabolome composition may include by-products that affect viability and damage forms that reach and pass the detection thresholds during organism's aging (Phoenix and de Grey, 2007), but they likely represent only the tip of the iceberg of cumulative damage.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation about the limitations of detection methods.

claim: Differences in accumulation of individual metabolites were responsible for lifespan differences between dietary groups.
source: We further followed age-related trajectories of 1066 individual metabolites common to short- and long-living flies and found that the trajectories of most metabolites correlated between the two dietary groups, yet varied in magnitude from initial to final concentration changes, suggesting that differences in accumulation of individual metabolites, in addition to the overall pattern, were responsible for lifespan differences.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of metabolite trajectories between dietary groups.

claim: Metabolites may exhibit diverse lifespan-regulatory roles similarly to genes.
source: Thus, metabolites, similarly to genes, may exhibit diverse lifespan-regulatory roles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similarity in patterns between metabolite and gene expression changes with age.

claim: Gradual transitions in thousands of nontargeted metabolites may be used to derive a signature that predicts survivorship across variable lifespans.
source: Similarly to targeted metabolite profiling in mammals (Tomas-Loba et al., 2013), the gradual transitions in thousands of nontargeted metabolites may be used to derive a signature that predicts survivorship across variable lifespans.
evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the observed correlations between metabolite patterns and survivorship, supported by citation to similar work in mammals.

claim: A significant overlap between metabolites that show age-associated changes between the diets can identify the biological, rather than the chronological, aging component.
source: A significant overlap between metabolites that show age-associated changes between the diets can also identify the biological, rather than the chronological, aging component.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the analysis of common age-associated metabolites between dietary groups.

claim: The aging process emerges as a gradual, dynamic metabolome remodeling that involves changes in the levels of numerous cellular metabolites.
source: Overall, from the current study the aging process emerges as a gradual, dynamic metabolome remodeling that involves changes in the levels (both increases and decreases) in numerous cellular metabolites, delays in these changes in late life and under conditions that lead to longer lifespan, and accumulation of damage, whose condition-dependent cumulative effects may impact survivorship.
evidence: The claim represents a major conclusion synthesizing multiple findings from the study.
